name: Familiarity heuristic
statement: When two objects are both recognised, people infer that the more familiar one ranks higher on whatever is being judged.
meaning: Three different claims travel under this name and they do not share a literature. The first is the one bias lists print. Wikipedia's article of that name says the familiar is favoured over novel places, people or things, and defines the heuristic as judging events more frequent or important because they are more familiar in memory. That definition is the availability heuristic, entry 38. No paper was found that defines or tests the claim under the familiarity name. The second is a rule for binary choice, proposed by Hidehito Honda and colleagues and modelled formally: given two cities, pick the more familiar as the larger. That rule generalises Goldstein and Gigerenzer's recognition heuristic, which can only fire when one of the two objects is unrecognised, and it has been tested against knowledge-based models. The third is the cue-familiarity heuristic in metamemory, where the familiarity of a question, rather than anything retrieved about its answer, drives the feeling of knowing the answer. The second and third claims each have evidence. Neither of them is the first one.

origin.note: Their paper is "The role of familiarity in binary choice inferences" and it calls the rule familiarity-based inference. Honda's later papers call the same rule the familiarity heuristic. The cue-familiarity heuristic of metamemory is older and separate: Koriat and Levy-Sadot's abstract traces it to Reder's 1987 paper on strategy selection in question answering.

evidence: Honda and colleagues ran two experiments on city populations. In the first, 33 undergraduates, all women, at Japan Women's University rated how familiar city names were and then chose which of two cities was larger. The mean proportion of choices agreeing with familiarity-based inference was 0.791, SD = 0.105. In the second, 81 undergraduates from the same university split into three clusters by how sensitive they were to small differences in familiarity, with mean agreement of 0.865, SD = 0.046, then 0.623, SD = 0.092, then 0.764, SD = 0.058. Their abstract reports that where participants had cue knowledge about population, they used it instead of familiarity. Honda, Matsuka and Ueda then set heuristic models against knowledge-based models on the same kind of task. Their abstract reports that a familiarity heuristic model explained inferences on tasks participants found subjectively difficult, and a knowledge-based model explained the ones they found easy. The metamemory strand is separate work. Metcalfe, Schwartz and Joaquim repeated cue words a varying number of times while holding the memorability of the targets apart from that count. Their paper reports four experiments and the figures here are from the first, run on 30 introductory psychology students at Dartmouth College. Across the A-B A-B, A-B' A-B, A-D A-B and C-D A-B conditions, cued recall ran .39, .33, .17 and .19, and recognition hit rates ran .72, .56, .59 and .48. Feeling-of-knowing ratings tracked neither, following instead the number of times the cue had been shown, F(3, 87) = 12.64, MSe = 83.13.

examples.tag: Two towns on the same map
examples.text: Asked which of two towns has more people, a traveller names the one she feels she knows better, having passed through it often. Both are recognised, so the sense of knowing one better is what settles the comparison.
A shopper asked to say which of two markets is the busier picks the one she visits every week. Her weekly habit, and not anything she knows about either market's trade, carries the judgement.

Asked which of two remedies is more widely used, a customer names the one whose packet feels more familiar. The extra familiarity comes from her own exposure rather than from how many other people buy it.

replication.headline: An independent laboratory in Ohio reproduced the binary-choice rule with different cities and a formal model, and the more familiar of two invented city names took 62% of choices in one study and 53% in the other.
replication.detail: Xu, González-Vallejo, Weinhardt, Chimeli and Karadogan tested the familiarity difference cue on Ohio cities rather than Japanese ones. Their stimuli were 24 large Ohio cities, 24 small ones and 24 invented names. In their first study, 113 Ohio University undergraduates rated familiarity and then made 72 paired choices about city size. Of the 113, 111 showed a significant positive correlation between city size and their own familiarity ratings, which is 98.23%. The invented names are the clean test, because nothing can be known about a city that does not exist. Of 1,356 pairs of two invented names, 944 were rated equally familiar. Of the remaining 412, participants chose the more familiar name 255 times, or 62%. Their second study, on 50 psychology undergraduates, put the same tendency at 104 of 194 cases, or 53%. The r-s multinomial model fitted both, G-squared(3) = 4.41, p = .22 in the first study and G-squared(3) = 1.23, p = .75 in the second. Their conclusion is that participants ignored further knowledge in a substantial number of cases when the familiarity difference cue was available. Response times were shorter for heuristic judgments than for judgments made on knowledge. What has been reproduced is the narrow rule about comparative judgment. The bias-list claim, that the familiar is favoured over the novel across places, people and things, was not tested by any of this work.

study.cite: Xu, P., González-Vallejo, C., Weinhardt, J., Chimeli, J., & Karadogan, F. (2018). Use of the familiarity difference cue in inferential judgments. Memory & Cognition, 46(2), 298-314.

limits: The rule is bounded by knowledge on one side and by its own materials on the other. Honda and colleagues report that cue knowledge about population displaced familiarity where participants had it, and Honda, Matsuka and Ueda report that the knowledge-based model won on tasks people found easy. Every study named here judges the size of cities. Familiarity is measured by asking the same person who then makes the choice, so cue and criterion come from one source. The samples are 33 and 81 women at one Japanese university and 113 and 50 undergraduates at Ohio University. No meta-analysis and no multi-laboratory replication of the familiarity heuristic was located. On the bias-list claim, that familiar things are favoured over novel ones, no paper was found that states and tests it under that name. The search was run again on 21 September 2026, at Crossref by bibliographic query for the phrase, at PubMed by title search, which returned no records at all, and by general web search, which returned popular explainers. The Wikipedia article of that name cites nine references, and none of them carries the phrase in its title or studies a thing so called. Honda's 2020 analysis of how forgetting affects the heuristic is an ACT-R model, published as a contributed article in a Keio University philosophy journal, and its abstract reports computer simulations rather than new human data.
misreadings: The commonest error is to run the arrow backwards. Monin reports five studies in which positive valence raises how familiar something feels with no prior exposure at all, so that attractive faces feel familiar, and he calls this the warm glow heuristic. His own abstract shares the credit with prototypicality, which it says accounts for only part of the face result. Wikipedia's familiarity heuristic article cites that paper. Liking causing felt familiarity is not familiarity causing liking, and only the second is what the name promises. A second error is treating the rule as the recognition heuristic under another label. Goldstein and Gigerenzer's heuristic fires on missing knowledge, when one object is recognised and the other is not, and the familiarity rule was proposed for the pairs the recognition heuristic cannot reach. A third is borrowing the availability literature. Judging a class more frequent because famous instances come to mind is Tversky and Kahneman's own study 8, which this atlas records under the availability heuristic, and it is not evidence for a separate rule. A fourth is treating the metamemory strand as the same thing. Its central prediction has taken a hit that the binary-choice strand has not. Oliver, Li, Harley and Humphreys ran three experiments, and their abstract reports that tip-of-the-tongue states repeated as readily when the retest prompt differed from the first prompt, which it calls inconsistent with the cue familiarity hypothesis, and that adding a semantic cue did not change the repeat rate either. A fifth is folding the rule into the fluency heuristic, entry 245, which turns on how fast an object is recognised. Honda, Matsuka and Ueda ran competitive tests of fluency and familiarity heuristic models, and Xu and colleagues say in their abstract that their paper discusses how the familiarity difference cue differs from the fluency heuristic.
